messages.author: 06b57f25e554a736
messages.subject: NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
parts:
The notebook in this repository shows the results of a very simple one parameter Bernoulli model with NUTS and ADVI.

https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/blob/master/stanadvi.ipynb

The trivial model is taken from the cmdstan manual (although the for loop has been replaced with a vectorized version).

The notebook only uses pystan to write the data in R format. The stan compilation and execution is handled by an up to date pull of the develop branch of cmdstan. You should be able to reproduce the results by doing `git clone --recursive https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/` then doing `make stan-update` in the cmdstan directory, then running the notebook.

The NUTS results are great: the MAP estimate of p pretty much exactly matches the true value nine times out of nine, and the width of the posterior is within 2 signifiant figures of the expected (frequentist) width sqrt(p*(1-p)/N).

The ADVI results are not as good. Agreement with the true value is rare, and the posterior mean and variance varies from run to run.

I have a bunch of questions:
 1) in situations where I don't know the right answer, how would I be able to tell something has gone wrong here? Is the ELBO score a clue? Is the eta adaptation weird? Is it strange that it converges after a couple of hundred iterations?
 2) what's a good ELBO score? The larger the better? Are the values seen here (-6e3) a sign of a problem?
 3) are there command line parameters I could use to fix this particular problem?
 4) is ADVI simply not appropriate for this problem? If so, given the trivial nature of the model (and that it is the first example in the cmdstan model), what kind of model would be OK with ADVI?
 5) or is ADVI as implemented in (cmd)stan not ready for public consumption without great care over convergence/initialization? NUTS seems pretty idiot proof, but is that less true of ADVI?

And a bonus question, which is I think unrelated to this problem: why isn't the example listing on p9 of the the cmdstan manual vectorized? What's with the for loop? :-)

Thanks,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
parts:
HI, Mike.  It's good to have this sort of example.  My quick answer is that the way to check that ADVi is giving reasonable results is by simulating fake data from the fitted model.  We are currently working on general guidelines for this idea.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
parts:
NUTS doesn't provide a MAP estimate. Optimization provides
the MAP estimate. You also don't get the frequentist posterior
interval. The posterior for the simple Bernoulli is a beta
distribution, and it's not even symmetric unless alpha = beta.

Your question (1) is the key thing we've been asking ourselves.

Alas, NUTS isn't completely robust, but we've tagged ADVI
as experimental (I hope that's clear in the interfaces), precisely
because we don't know how to characterize when it will work or
how to make it signal that it's gone wrong.

- Bob

Thanks! My point in mentioning "MAP" (which I misused: I just meant the mean and width of the posterior) was to note that the NUTS posteriors are stable from run to run, and in approximately the right place, which is not true of the ADVI estimates.

Mike

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
parts:
Intuitively, ADVI works best when the target distribution (i.e. your posterior)
is Gaussian without too many correlations.  How is degrades as the target
becomes less Gaussian or the correlations grow is an open question.  In
particular, there are low-dimensional models where ADVI works poorly
and high-dimesnional models where ADVI works okay.  In general, however,
it can struggle on the kinds of complex models for which Stan was originally
designed.

You hit on an even more important, point, however, in that we don’t yet have
a strong theoretical understanding of how to check whether ADVI will work
beforehand or how to verify that ADVI worked after the fact (unlike HMC/
NUTS where we’ve been developing a wealth of theoretical and empirical 
understanding).  One of the strong motivations for including ADVI in Stan 
was to do simulation tests like yours to build up a preliminary empirical 
understanding of when ADVI might work and when it might not.  The early 
results are consistent with the above intuition, but still not quite generic enough 
to really inform practice (at least in my opinion).  Also in my opinion, the limitations
are more to do with the limitation of the assumed variational distributions than
any of the particulars in the ADVI implementation itself.

This lack of understanding is why we list ADVI as “experimental” and warn
against its use in production analysis.

Thanks! My point in mentioning "MAP" (which I misused: I just meant the mean and width of the posterior) was to note that the NUTS posteriors are stable from run to run, and in approximately the right place, which is not true of the ADVI estimates.

So for now it seems like ADVI can't be used for very simple problems that appear in the documentation. Do you happen to know if that's an inherent limitation of the algorithm, or of Stan's implementation?

Mike

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
parts:
Variational inference is a very general technique that arguably
includes EP as well as the various forms of hand-tuned VB (custom
approximations to go with the models).

ADVI uses a multivariate normal (diagonal or dense covariance)
approximation to the posterior and some other approximations for
computing (Alp's paper is super clear on all this). As far
as we know, there aren't bugs in the implementations and we don't
suspect implementations are an issue.

So this doesn't say anything much about how other variational
inference schemes might or might not work.

- Bob

Thanks all! Some of this discussion went a little over my head, but I'm glad to know I wasn't doing anything stupid, and this is work in progress!

Mike

On Wednesday, 22 June 2016 17:26:27 UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
And this is why we're excited about the research project of developing methods to use targeted fake-data simulation to detect problems with ADVI and other approximations!

On Jun 22, 2016, at 9:45 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

Intuitively, ADVI works best when the target distribution (i.e. your posterior)
is Gaussian without too many correlations.  How is degrades as the target
becomes less Gaussian or the correlations grow is an open question.  In
particular, there are low-dimensional models where ADVI works poorly
and high-dimesnional models where ADVI works okay.  In general, however,
it can struggle on the kinds of complex models for which Stan was originally
designed.

You hit on an even more important, point, however, in that we don’t yet have
a strong theoretical understanding of how to check whether ADVI will work
beforehand or how to verify that ADVI worked after the fact (unlike HMC/
NUTS where we’ve been developing a wealth of theoretical and empirical 
understanding).  One of the strong motivations for including ADVI in Stan 
was to do simulation tests like yours to build up a preliminary empirical 
understanding of when ADVI might work and when it might not.  The early 
results are consistent with the above intuition, but still not quite generic enough 
to really inform practice (at least in my opinion).  Also in my opinion, the limitations
are more to do with the limitation of the assumed variational distributions than
any of the particulars in the ADVI implementation itself.

This lack of understanding is why we list ADVI as “experimental” and warn
against its use in production analysis.

messages.author: 06b57f25e554a736
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
parts:
Hi Alp,

thank you very much for your reply! I hope you don't mind if I bother you with some belated follow-up questions...

> On Jun 22, 2016, at 14:34, Alp Kucukelbir <a...@cs.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> hi michael,
>
> first of all, thank you for this study. as others mentioned, this is
> one of the main reasons why we are excited to have advi in stan.

sure! I learned a lot even boiling things down to a minimal example :-)

> second, i'm not sure the results are as dire as in your study. you are
> comparing the empircial posterior mean, while in advi we actually have
> access to the variational posterior mean. (a quick replication of your
> study on my end shows that these are closer to the nuts estimate.)

How do you mean? If you run the notebook with no changes do you get better agreement between the two approaches? Certainly I see variation from run to run (especially in the ADVI output, which is itself a concern for me), but the one invariant is that, of the 9 runs of ADVI, at least 2 or 3 of them will be severely off, in the sense that the "true" value is right at the edge of the variational posterior distribution, which never happens for NUTS.

> [also see the package `pip install stanhelper`. this simplifies many
> of the tasks you are doing by interfacing cmdstan with python]

Thanks! That's certainly simpler than installing pystan. But does this library just handle the dump to R format and reading from a CSV file? Is there something more to it?

> third, let me try to answer some of your questions.

>
>> 1) in situations where I don't know the right answer, how would I be able to tell something has gone wrong here? Is the ELBO score a clue? Is the eta adaptation weird? Is it strange that it converges after a couple of hundred iterations?
>

> making sure the ELBO has converged is the first step.
>
> i'm not sure what constitutes "weird".

I wasn't sure if it was significant that the optimal eta turned out to be the first guess (1), and that it was "found earlier than expected", which sounds a little ominous.

> the ELBO can take anything from tens to millions of iterations to
> converge, depending on the model.

But in the case of this model it has converged satisfactorily, right?

>> 3) are there command line parameters I could use to fix this particular problem?
>

> yes. a lower threshold improves accuracy in this toy model.

Sorry, which threshold? I couldn't find anything relevant in the cmdstan or stan manuals.

Mike

messages.author: 06b57f25e554a736
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
parts: Hi Alp,

On Jul 1, 2016, at 09:28, Alp Kucukelbir <a...@cs.columbia.edu> wrote:
>> But in the case of this model it has converged satisfactorily, right?
>

> one way to check this is to plot the elbo. it should look relatively
